Seafood / Restaurant

Spicy Grilled Nakji Octopus

Nakji is the small octopus of the nakji-bokkeum tradition — the fierce stir-fried classic — and this record is that flavor set run over live fire instead of a screaming wok.

Korean · Medium · Serves 3–4

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 02 / 15 seafood recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant. Nakji is the small octopus of the nakji-bokkeum tradition — the fierce stir-fried classic — and this record is that flavor set run over live fire instead of a screaming wok. The technique difference matters more than the flavor one: a whole small octopus (about 300 g each) is too thick to stay tender at grill speed, so it needs either the old-school pounding or a brief pre-simmer before the grill. This record runs the simmer-then-grill path — the home-kitchen-honest one — and the gochujang glaze lands in the final minute, same law as the squid record (#SF04).

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The pre-simmer is the tenderizing — do not skip it for the fire's sake. Bring the salted, gingered water to a boil, drop in the octopus, and simmer exactly 4 minutes for small ones. Lift, cool under running water, and drain. The flesh is now tender-set and the grill's job is color and glaze only. Skipping this and grilling raw is how nakji becomes a rubber band.
  • Slice after the simmer: body into wide rings or opened flat into sheets (scored lightly in a crosshatch, the #SF04 law), tentacles in halves lengthwise. Pat thoroughly dry.
  • Whisk the glaze and park it at the grill station. Fire at medium-high.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Dry slices onto the hot grate in a single layer, 90 seconds undisturbed — you are searing color onto already-cooked octopus, so every second is flavor, not doneness. Checkpoint — char marks on the faces and edges, the scored sheets curling open. The smell is toast over the ocean — clean and sweet.
  2. 02
    Flip, brush the seared faces with glaze, 45–60 seconds, second brush-stroke, off the fire. Total grill time under 3 minutes — the simmer did the cooking and the glaze only needs to set. Checkpoint — glossy brick-red slices, char at the edges. The eating test at the grill station: tender-chewy with a snap that yields (nakji's correct texture — firmer than squid, never rubber), sweet-heat over octopus depth.
  3. 03
    Platter, sesame over, and the table eats it over rice with the cold crunchy banchan beside. Checkpoint — the bowl test: glaze-slicked nakji over rice with bean sprouts in the same bite — heat, chew, crunch. If every bite is all glaze, the slices were too small; wide pieces carry the balance. Chef’s Note — the old alternative to the pre-simmer is the pounding board: the street vendors of the nakji tradition hammer the whole octopus with a mallet or daikon bat until the flesh relaxes — mechanical tenderizing, the same idea as the neobiani knife work (#M08) applied to an octopus. It works, it is theatrical, and it takes a strong arm and ten honest minutes per octopus. The simmer is the calmer road to the same tenderness, with the small trade that the octopus loses a little of its juice to the pot — the glaze gives it back.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Rubber-band chewRaw octopus grilled, or over-grilledThe 4-minute simmer; under 3 minutes on the fire
Glaze burntGlazed at the startGlaze after the flip, 45 seconds
Watery, no charOctopus wet from the simmerCool, drain, pat dry twice
Bland under the glazeUnder-simmered (no salt/ginger)The pre-simmer is seasoned — do not simmer in plain water

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Simmered octopus keeps 2 days refrigerated before grilling — the record's make-ahead is built in. Cooked, 2 days, into fried rice or noodles.
  • Variations: the no-simmer pounding path (see Note); baby octopus skips the slicing and runs whole on the jjukkumi record (#SF06); the glaze doubles on the squid record (#SF04).
